newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Bank of Zambia says economic outlook encouraging.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Zambia says economic outlook encouraging.

text.p: Zambia's economic future looked encouraging but there was some concern about stability when the country's elections take place later this month, the central Bank of Zambia said on Thursday.
"The general outlook is encouraging because of the expansion of non-mineral exports," Bank of Zambia governor Jacob Mwanza told Reuters.

Mwanza said in an interview that increased exports of agriculture products were helping to improve the economy which in the past relied on copper and cobalt exports for about 80 percent of the country's exports.
"This has in a way helped us to maintain stability in the exchange rate," he said.
The Zambian kwacha has weakened from less than 1,000 kwacha to the dollar in January to around 1,258 kwacha in October, but has been trading steadily around present levels since May.
Zambia's economic reforms since President Frederick Chiluba's government came to power in 1991 had helped create a climate for investment, Mwanza added.
But he said there was some concern about elections due to take place on November 18.
Former president Kenneth Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP) and six other opposition parties are boycotting the elections.
"I see it as a potential area of conflict in the event that UNIP succeeds in what they are trying to do, which is to undermine the country.
"My own assessment is that there should be some temporary short-term impact but fundamentals are likely to remain intact," Mwanza said.
Mwanza said interest rates were likely to come down from the official Bank of Zambia rate of 67.5 percent in October and he also predicted a drop in inflation -- currently at around 46.3 percent.
"I see that the stabilisation will deepen. Interest rates will definitely start going down, inflation must go down," he said.
Mwanza said Zambia's privatisation process, including the sale of copper mines, would increase the country's foreign exchange reserves.
International aid donors, including the United States, Japan, Britain and Scandanavian countries suspended aid in June over the government's move to bar Kaunda from contesting this month's elections.
"We will in the short term increase our foreign exchange inflows by the sale of the mines," Mwanza said.
Zambia's largest company, Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd (ZCCM), is up for sale and 39 foreign companies have pre-qualified to buy the mining and power assets of ZCCM.
